query: For a multicomponent high-entropy alloy in its high-temperature solid and liquid states, what single intervention could overcome the limited accuracy, availability, and efficiency of determining melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change upon melting, and liquid thermodynamic properties across a large compositional space? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention and causal mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to current experimental and computational baselines, defines the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes a decisive falsification test against independent reference data.

generation.hypothesis: The intervention of using high-throughput computational modeling, specifically incorporating first-principles calculations and thermophysical parameter calculations, can overcome the limited accuracy, availability, and efficiency of determining melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change upon melting, and liquid thermodynamic properties across a large compositional space for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys in their high-temperature solid and liquid states
generation.intervention: Using high-throughput computational modeling incorporating first-principles calculations and thermophysical parameter calculations
generation.mechanism: High-throughput computational models can efficiently predict phase stability and thermodynamic properties, enhancing the accuracy and availability of these properties across a large compositional space
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved accuracy, availability, and efficiency in determining melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change upon melting, and liquid thermodynamic properties
generation.boundary: Limited to high-entropy alloys and high-temperature conditions
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty in the accuracy of high-throughput computational models for predicting phase stability and thermodynamic properties

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of high-throughput computational models with experimental data for a range of high-entropy alloys
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-throughput computational models do not accurately predict the measured properties within a specified error margin, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Intervention effect. Base system: Polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy in face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures. Intervention: Accounting for longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature in first-principles calculations. Processing: First-principles alloy theory using DFT with the LSF methodology (Dong et al.) and fluctuating medium approximation. Test conditions: Temperature range 50 K to 1200 K; volumes represented by Wigner-Seitz radius. Structure change: Finite magnetic moments thermally induced for Co, Cr, and Ni at all volumes even at 50 K; mean magnetic moments {m_I} exhibit monotonic dependency on volume and temperature. Property change: Magnetic moments for Co, Cr, and Ni increase with temperature; e.g., at 100 K, m_Co is 0.73 μ_B (fcc) and 0.67 μ_B (hcp); at 900 K, m_Co is 1.30 μ_B (fcc) and 1.27 μ_B (hcp). Mechanism: LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr, and Ni, whereas Fe and Mn already have large spontaneous static magnetic moments. Evidence: simulated. Quote: "Accounting for the LSFs at finite temperature (contour plots in Fig. 1), finite magnetic moments have been thermally induced for Cr, Ni and C

Intervention effect. Base system: PM CoCrFeMnNi. Intervention: Evaluation of magnetic moments {m_I} as a function of temperature with thermal lattice expansion. Processing: LSF calculations combined with experimental thermal lattice expansion data. Test conditions: Temperatures 100 K, 300 K, and 900 K. Structure change: Mean magnetic moments {m_I} in both phases significantly increase with temperature. Property change: At 100 K, difference in m_I between fcc and hcp phases amounts to ~0.05, 0.03, 0.17, and 0.23 μ_B for Co, Cr, Fe, and Mn respectively. Mechanism: The m_I of Fe and Mn shows more pronounced dependency on volume with respect to that on temperature, whereas LSFs give the prevailing contribution to the m_I of Co, Cr and Ni. Evidence: simulated. Quote: "It is evident that { m I } in both phases significantly increase with temperature, and at the given temperatures the magnetic states of the alloy components in the fcc phase are very close to those in the hcp phase."
